data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A decentralized network is NOT more resilient than a large redundant service when a shared external market signal synchronizes the independent operators into identical failure modes, creating self-organized criticality.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If small operators are provably unaware of each other's market positions and use diverse, non-convergent scaling algorithms, the synchronization mechanism fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the large service lacks internal architectural diversity and uses a single scaling policy, it fails in the same way as the synchronized network.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Independent operators optimizing for the same market metrics (e.g., cost-per-request) converge on identical auto-scaling thresholds and configurations. During stable periods, they appear uncorrelated. However, under a specific market stress (e.g., a price spike in compute), all small services simultaneously hit their scaling limits and trigger the same cost-saving reboot/failover procedure. The shared cause (the market signal) induces correlated failure across 'independent' nodes, whereas a single large service can enforce internal diversity (different teams, codebases, and thresholds) to prevent synchronous behavior.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
